blocks.text: A butcher's tray in a Lagos market holds a goat's foreleg, a chicken wing and a fish head. Strip them to bone and the goat's limb still shares the same one-bone, two-bones, many-bones, five-digit plan as your own arm. That pentadactyl layout is a family resemblance left by common ancestry — one of several independent lines of evidence that species have changed, and are related.

blocks.markdown:
## The fossil record

A **fossil** is the preserved remains, impression or trace of an organism, usually in sedimentary rock. Shells, bones, teeth, footprints and even leaf prints can fossilise when an organism is buried quickly and minerals replace the tissues.

**Relative dating** uses position: older layers lie deeper, younger layers nearer the surface, so a fossil's age can be ranked against others in the same cliff. **Absolute dating** uses radioactive isotopes (for example carbon-14 in recent remains, uranium in older rock) to estimate age in years.

The record is incomplete — soft bodies rarely fossilise, and many rocks have been eroded — but the pattern is consistent: simpler organisms appear in older rocks, more complex ones later, and transitional forms (such as feathered dinosaurs, or early whales with hind-limb bones) sit where the theory of descent predicts.

blocks.title: Homologous structures
blocks.text: Organs that share the same basic plan and embryonic origin, even if their present functions differ, because they were inherited from a common ancestor. The pentadactyl limb of a human, a bat, a whale and a horse is the standard example: one upper bone, two lower bones, a set of wrist bones, and five (or modified) digits.

rows: Same underlying structure, possibly different functions
Pentadactyl limb of human, bat, whale, horse
Wing of an insect and wing of a bird; fin of a shark and flipper of a dolphin
Similar selection, not recent common ancestry (convergent evolution)
Reduced structure with little or no current function
Human appendix and coccyx; pelvic bones of a whale; hind-limb remnants in some snakes
The ancestor used the full structure
blocks.caption: Homologous, analogous and vestigial — keep these three words distinct

blocks.markdown:
## Adaptive radiation and other evidence

**Adaptive radiation** is the evolution of several species from one ancestral stock, each fitted to a different niche. Darwin's finches on the Galápagos islands are the classic case: one ancestral finch gave rise to species with crushing, probing or picking beaks according to diet. Closer to home, **cichlid fishes** in West African rivers and crater lakes have radiated into algae-grazers, insect-pickers and fish-eaters from shared ancestors — the same pattern in a Nigerian-region fauna.

**Comparative embryology.** Early vertebrate embryos look strikingly alike (gill pouches, a tail), which is hard to explain unless they share an ancestor.

**Comparative biochemistry.** The more recently two species split, the more similar their DNA, cytochrome c and haemoglobin sequences. Humans and chimpanzees are closer on this measure than humans and lizards, matching the anatomical evidence.

items: Fossils give a time sequence and occasional missing-link forms; they do not have to be complete to be useful.
Homologous organs argue for divergence from a common plan; analogous organs argue for convergence on a similar job.
Vestigial organs are leftover homologies that selection has reduced rather than removed.
Adaptive radiation shows how one ancestral species can fill many niches when new habitats open.
Embryology and molecular sequences independently support the same family tree as anatomy and fossils.

blocks.title: Classifying three pairs of structures
blocks.prompt: Classify each pair as homologous, analogous or vestigial evidence, and state what evolutionary process each illustrates: (i) the forelimb of a goat and the wing of a fruit bat; (ii) the wing of a fruit bat and the wing of a locust; (iii) the pelvic bones inside a whale.

steps.text: Goat forelimb and bat wing both show the pentadactyl plan (humerus, radius and ulna, wrist, digits), even though one walks and the other flies. They are homologous — evidence of common ancestry and divergent evolution.

A bat wing is skin stretched on pentadactyl bones; a locust wing is a chitinous flap moved by a different set of muscles and with no bones. Same job (flight), different structure: analogous — convergent evolution.
A whale's pelvic bones do not support hind legs, yet they match the pelvis of land mammals. They are vestigial homologies, leftover from a walking ancestor.

blocks.answer: (i) Homologous (divergence). (ii) Analogous (convergence). (iii) Vestigial (reduced homology from a terrestrial ancestor).

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: Homologous = same plan, different job, common ancestor. Analogous = same job, different plan, no recent common ancestor for that organ. Students regularly swap those two. Name the pentadactyl limb for homology and insect wing versus bird wing for analogy. For adaptive radiation, Darwin's finches or West African cichlids both earn the mark if you mention one ancestor and several niches.

points: Fossils in sedimentary rock, dated by position and by radioisotopes, show that life has changed through time.
Homologous structures such as the pentadactyl limb indicate common ancestry; analogous structures such as insect and bird wings indicate convergent evolution.
Vestigial organs (appendix, whale pelvis) are reduced remnants of ancestral structures.
Adaptive radiation — Darwin's finches, West African cichlids — produces many species from one ancestor as niches are filled.
Embryology and comparative biochemistry independently support the same relationships as anatomy and the fossil record.
